claims.text: Adding a controlled low concentration of interstitial carbon to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its strength–plasticity balance.
The proposed starting RHEA has a stable FCC matrix and lacks significant interstitial alloying.
Approximately 0.5 at% carbon is a feasible low-concentration interstitial addition.
Carbon addition increases the stacking-fault energy and phase stability of an FCC high-entropy-alloy matrix.
Tuning FCC phase stability to a critical point can activate TWIP while retaining TRIP.
At the selected carbon concentration, significant brittle-carbide formation will be avoided.
Interstitial carbon produces lattice distortion and interstitial solid-solution strengthening through enhanced interaction with dislocations.
Simultaneous TWIP and TRIP activation improves strain hardening.
The carbon-doped RHEA will have higher yield strength than the carbon-free reference processed and tested identically.
The carbon-doped RHEA will have greater uniform elongation than the carbon-free reference.
The proposed TWIP/TRIP enhancement will operate during room-temperature tensile deformation of the carbon-doped RHEA.
The benefit exists only within an optimal carbon-concentration window.
Excess carbon may cause carbide precipitation that reduces ductility and offsets strength gains.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility relative to the carbon-free control would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of increased twin density or martensitic transformation in the carbon-doped alloy would falsify the proposed TWIP/TRIP mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial matrix is described as stable FCC, whereas the proposed TRIP mechanism requires an FCC matrix sufficiently metastable to undergo a strain-induced martensitic transformation.
